There are four ways to get one: buy a platform, assemble it from parts, self-host the stack, or have one built and operated inside your environment. Ramp and Uber built theirs with platform teams. Here is what each route costs in engineering time.\n\n## What an AI software factory is made of\n\n![Banner of the factory line: a ticket feeds sandbox, agent, and QA stations and comes out as a pull request with evidence](https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/54b81b237393d8e81463c55c/debc201b-79d0-4fd7-817f-b07564d275a3.png align=\"center\")\n\nEvery product in this category runs the same five-stage loop, so it is the most useful way to organise the tooling.\n\n1.  **Intake.** Work arrives as a ticket, spec, or logged bug rather than as a prompt typed into an editor.\n    \n2.  **Isolation.** A sandbox spins up, clones the repositories, and is destroyed when the run ends.\n    \n3.  **Implementation.** A coding agent does the work inside that sandbox.\n    \n4.  **Verification.** The run executes the repository's own checks, and for user-facing changes drives a real browser.\n    \n5.  **The pull request.** One PR per changed repository, with the diff and the evidence attached. A human reviews and merges.\n    \n\n![The AI software factory loop: intake from Linear, Jira, or GitHub Issues, an isolated sandbox, a coding agent implementing the change, verification through repo checks and recorded browser QA with a retry loop on failure, and one evidence-backed pull request per changed repo for human review](https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/54b81b237393d8e81463c55c/22d42980-de73-4649-9875-8a7fe481ac4d.png align=\"center\")\n\nWe covered the category argument and who is claiming what in [a separate piece on the AI software factory](https://hashnode.com/blog/ai-software-factory). This one is about the parts.\n\nOne disambiguation before the tools. If you arrived here from a government or defence context, \"software factory\" there still means the 2010s DevSecOps meaning: accredited platforms and teams like Kessel Run and Platform One, with golden pipelines and continuous authority to operate. Humans still write the software in those. Same name, different architecture, and the rest of this article is about the agent-era sense.\n\n## The teams who built their own\n\n![Banner naming the two in-house software factories: Ramp's Inspect and Uber's Minion](https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/54b81b237393d8e81463c55c/c3ba3b93-ea9d-47b7-ac87-ae6a48903df0.png align=\"center\")\n\nTwo things are worth knowing before you evaluate anything, because they establish that this works and what it costs.\n\nRamp built an internal background coding agent called Inspect. Their engineering post states that [~30% of all pull requests merged to their frontend and backend repos are written by Inspect](https://builders.ramp.com/post/why-we-built-our-background-agent). The architecture is worth reading directly: each session runs in a sandboxed VM on Modal \"with everything an engineer would have locally: Vite, Postgres, Temporal, the works,\" from repository images pre-built every 30 minutes, with filesystem snapshots to freeze and restore state.\n\nUber built Minion, an agent platform wired into their monorepo. Their published figures via The Pragmatic Engineer put [92% of Uber devs using agents monthly and 11% of pull requests opened by agents](https://newsletter.pragmaticengineer.com/p/how-uber-uses-ai-for-development). The detailed Minion numbers sit behind that newsletter's paywall, so treat anything more specific you see quoted elsewhere with suspicion.\n\nNeither company bought this. There was nothing to buy. Both assigned platform teams to build agent infrastructure: sandboxing, credential handling, and review workflow. It worked, which is the useful part. The software factory model is proven. What the two cases also establish is the price of the proof: a platform team.\n\nKeep that in mind through the next three sections, because the tiers below are mostly a question of who does that work.\n\n## Tier 1: buy a platform\n\n![Banner for tier 1, buying an AI software factory platform off the shelf](https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/54b81b237393d8e81463c55c/83983791-7dd1-4310-95c0-3c51f7c68d54.png align=\"center\")\n\nThe turnkey option. Every claim in this table is the vendor's own, taken from their site, and none of it is independently measured.\n\n| Product | Company | Their pitch, their words | Deployment |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| [Devin](https://cognition.com) | Cognition | \"The first autonomous software engineer\" | Enterprise; named customers include Goldman Sachs and Mercedes-Benz |\n| [Factory](https://factory.ai) | Factory | \"A self-improving system for your SDLC\" | SaaS, hybrid, on-prem, air-gapped |\n| [8090](https://8090.ai) | 8090 | \"The AI-native software factory for regulated enterprises\" | Self-serve platform plus custom enterprise builds |\n\nThere is also a lighter version of this tier hiding inside subscriptions you may already pay for. [GitHub Copilot's coding agent](https://github.blog/changelog/2025-09-25-copilot-coding-agent-is-now-generally-available/) has been generally available since September 2025: assign an issue to Copilot and it works in a cloud environment and returns a draft pull request, with a Linear integration added since. [Jules](https://jules.google/), Google's asynchronous coding agent, reached general availability at I/O 2026 and runs the same shape, task in, cloud VM, plan, PR out. Cursor runs background agents in its cloud as well. None of these carries the verification or credential plumbing of the dedicated platforms, but if the question is whether the ticket-to-PR loop fits your team at all, the cheapest experiment is one you already own.\n\nWhat you are buying from the dedicated platforms is the plumbing between the five stages. What you are not buying is the integration into your stack: your repositories, your CI, your ticketing conventions, your compliance posture. That work stays with you, and on a large codebase it is not small.\n\n## Tier 2: assemble it from parts\n\n![Banner for tier 2, assembling a software factory from sandbox, agent, and QA parts](https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/54b81b237393d8e81463c55c/5da1e1b4-bb5d-494c-8e45-8590416c3e42.png align=\"center\")\n\nThis is what Ramp and Uber did, and every layer of it is now purchasable separately. If you already pay for a coding agent and a CI provider, you are further along than you think.\n\n![The assemble-it-yourself software factory stack by layer: intake tools, agent sandboxes including E2B, Modal, Daytona, Northflank, and Vercel Sandbox, coding agents, verification with repo checks, Playwright, and Passmark, with credentials and orchestration brokered in from outside the flow](https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/54b81b237393d8e81463c55c/16527615-c8b7-420a-98b9-85d8749f66ca.png align=\"center\")\n\n### Intake\n\nLinear, Jira, GitHub Issues, or a Slack channel. There is no specialist tool here, and that is the point: the queue you already run is the queue the factory reads. The engineering work is in the trigger, deciding which labels or states hand a ticket to an agent.\n\n### Isolation\n\nThe agent sandbox is the layer teams underestimate, and the one Ramp singles out in their own writeup.\n\n| Sandbox | What it is built for |\n| --- | --- |\n| [E2B](https://e2b.dev) | Isolated sandboxes for agents to execute code, each a Linux VM created on demand |\n| [Modal](https://modal.com) | Secure containers for running untrusted user or agent code, defined at runtime instead of pre-deployed. This is what Ramp runs Inspect on |\n| [Daytona](https://daytona.io) | Development environments that persist across sessions instead of being torn down each run |\n| [Northflank](https://northflank.com) | Sandboxes for untrusted code with managed cloud or your own VPC |\n| [Vercel Sandbox](https://vercel.com/docs/vercel-sandbox) | Ephemeral sandboxes for running untrusted, agent-generated code on Vercel's infrastructure |\n\nA note on sourcing. Most of the head-to-head comparisons of these providers that rank on search are published by Northflank, which is one of the providers in the table. Their posts are useful and also not neutral. The specific isolation technology each uses (microVMs, gVisor, containers) is claimed more precisely in those comparisons than in the providers' own documentation, so verify against primary docs before you make a security decision on it.\n\n### Implementation\n\nThe agent that writes the code. Claude Code, Codex, and Grok cover the commercial end, and if you want to see how the first two differ in practice, FactoryKit's learn library [compares Claude Code and Codex](https://factorykit.ai/p/claude-code-vs-codex) from the vantage point of running both in production. On the open-source end sit Aider, Cline, OpenCode, [OpenHands](https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands), and [Goose](https://github.com/block/goose), the Apache 2.0 agent Block built and has since moved to the Linux Foundation.\n\nThe useful design decision here is not which agent to pick but whether to pick one at all. Models leapfrog each other on a timescale of weeks, and a factory that hard-codes one agent inherits that model's bad quarter.\n\n### Verification\n\nThe stage that separates a factory from an agent left running overnight, and the one most assembled stacks skip.\n\nRunning the repository's existing checks is the floor: lint, types, unit tests, whatever CI already does. The gap is everything a reviewer actually worries about, which is whether a user-facing change still works. [Playwright](https://playwright.dev) is the standard browser automation layer. [Passmark](https://github.com/bug0inc/passmark) is an open-source Playwright library for AI browser regression testing, with caching, auto-healing, and multi-model verification of assertions, which is the piece that makes browser QA survive a codebase that changes daily.\n\nGreen unit tests do not tell a reviewer whether the page a user sees still renders. Browser evidence does, and it is the part an assembled stack has to add deliberately.\n\n### Credentials\n\nInfisical, Doppler, or HashiCorp Vault will hold secrets. The architectural question matters more than the tool: does the agent ever hold a credential at all, or does something outside the sandbox attach them to outbound requests?\n\nAn agent with repository write access and a model key is a service with unusual reach and unpredictable behaviour. The [coding agent security](https://factorykit.ai/p/coding-agent-security) primer in FactoryKit's learn library covers the threat model, and the short version is that scoping matters more than sandboxing.\n\n### Orchestration\n\nRetries, long-running runs, and state that survives a process restart. Temporal is the common answer, and notably it appears inside Ramp's sandbox image as well.\n\n### What assembling actually costs\n\nEvery component above is available and most are good. The work is not in choosing them, it is in the joins: trigger logic, credential brokering, snapshot management, retry policy, and the review surface. That is a platform engineering project, it does not finish when the first run succeeds, and Ramp and Uber are the evidence for its scale rather than an argument against doing it.\n\n## Tier 3: self-host the whole stack\n\n![Banner for tier 3, a self-hosted software factory running inside your own network perimeter](https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/54b81b237393d8e81463c55c/7005a971-6c79-4e4e-ae59-4930a12966b4.png align=\"center\")\n\nFor teams whose code cannot go to a third party at all, whether for regulatory reasons or contractual ones.\n\nFor a self-hosted coding agent there are real open-source options: Aider, Cline, and OpenCode run against your own model keys, Goose runs entirely on your machine, and OpenHands ships an enterprise Kubernetes deployment. The isolation layer means running Firecracker, gVisor, or Kata Containers yourself rather than buying a sandbox service. Verification and orchestration are unchanged, since Playwright, Passmark, and Temporal are self-hostable already.\n\nWhat you gain is that nothing leaves your network. What you pay is that you now operate a microVM fleet in addition to everything in tier 2. This is the most expensive route in engineering time and the only viable one for some buyers.\n\n## Tier 4: have one built by forward-deployed engineers\n\n![Banner for tier 4, a forward-deployed engineering team installing a factory inside your infrastructure](https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/54b81b237393d8e81463c55c/4002052f-32ee-4b2f-abb2-1033c55c82ba.png align=\"center\")\n\nThe fourth route is the one the category rarely names, and it is a different axis from the first three rather than a fourth product.\n\nA forward-deployed engineer is an engineer who embeds with a customer to deploy and adapt a product inside the customer's own environment, rather than supporting it from the outside. Applied to this category, it means the vendor's engineers install the factory on your infrastructure, run it against your backlog, and hand it over.\n\nIn tiers 1, 2, and 3, the integration work belongs to the customer. A turnkey platform still has to be wired into your repositories and conventions. Assembling means building those joins. Self-hosting means building them and running the infrastructure underneath. At enterprise scale that integration is not the last mile, it is most of the project: which repos, which CI, which ticketing conventions, which compliance regime, where credentials are allowed to live. A platform ships the generic majority of a factory. The part that decides whether it gets used is specific to the buyer, and that is the part an embedded engineer builds.\n\nThe forward-deployed model moves both the integration and the operating burden to the vendor, inside the customer's environment, with custom builds part of the engagement rather than a roadmap item. This is what a software factory as a service properly means, and it is the difference between buying a factory and having one installed.\n\nThree properties make the model work for enterprises in a way the other tiers cannot. The factory runs in your cloud or fully on premises, so the data objection that disqualifies tier 1 for regulated buyers does not arise. The backlog is being cleared while the factory is being built, which no tier 2 project can offer, since those spend their first quarter shipping nothing but infrastructure. And the engagement is designed to end: the vendor's engineers hand the controls to your team and stay on maintenance, so what you own at the end is a factory, not a dependency on the people who built it.\n\n![The FactoryKit homepage: Ramp and Uber built their own coding-agent factories, you can just plug one in. The subhead describes plain-language tasks becoming evidence-backed pull requests, implemented by an isolated AI coding agent and QA'd in a recorded real browser](https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/54b81b237393d8e81463c55c/c9ab6c59-ac0f-4f36-97f1-8989628ceeaf.png align=\"center\")\n\n[FactoryKit](https://factorykit.ai), which is built by the team behind this publication, runs exactly this model: its forward-deployed engineers drive the factory on the customer's backlog for the first one to three months while it is built on their infrastructure, then hand it over and stay on maintenance under subscription. The architecture underneath:\n\n*   Each task runs in an isolated cloud sandbox. No local development environment is involved.\n    \n*   The coding agent is chosen per task: Claude Code, Codex, or Grok.\n    \n*   The agent never holds a real credential. Credentials are brokered into outbound traffic in transit, scoped per repository.\n    \n*   The agent never touches git. The platform commits, pushes, and opens one pull request per changed repository, so a multi-repo task returns coordinated PRs instead of one tangled diff.\n    \n*   Every user-facing change is regression tested in a real browser with Passmark, and the session recording is attached to the pull request.\n    \n*   Linear is connected today: label an issue, and the factory picks it up and answers on the ticket with a PR.\n    \n\n![A FactoryKit task that touched several repositories, showing one pull request opened in each changed repository rather than a single combined diff](https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/54b81b237393d8e81463c55c/9f22522f-2607-4b68-887b-388750de423a.png align=\"center\")\n\nThe recording is the part that is hard to picture from a bullet, so here is what actually lands on the pull request: the browser QA session for the change, attached to the PR a reviewer opens.\n\n![A FactoryKit pull request with the browser QA session recording attached, showing the regression test of the change as evidence for the reviewer](https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/54b81b237393d8e81463c55c/9b0b179f-2b23-44d1-a698-2cf8cb9ef9b6.png align=\"center\")\n\nThe limits. Standard web applications are the sweet spot and mobile is not supported. It is GitHub only, so GitLab teams are out for now. FactoryKit's own numbers put simple tasks at about five minutes, moderate ones at ten to fifteen, and complex ones at twenty to thirty. And a vague task produces a vague PR, which is the constraint every product in this category shares and few will print.\n\n## Which route are you actually on\n\n![Banner showing the four routes to an AI software factory: buy, assemble, self-host, or forward-deployed](https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/54b81b237393d8e81463c55c/670177a2-d617-4974-bfd2-3813c494250c.png align=\"center\")\n\n|  | Buy a platform | Assemble | Self-host | Forward-deployed |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| Time to first PR | Days | A quarter | Longer | Weeks |\n| Who integrates it | You | You | You | The vendor |\n| Who operates it | Vendor | You | You | Vendor, in your environment |\n| Code leaves your network | Yes | Depends | No | No |\n| Best fit | Speed matters most | You have platform engineers | Compliance forbids the rest | You want tier 2 without building it |\n\nMost teams evaluating tier 1 are actually choosing between tiers 1 and 4, and most teams evaluating tier 2 are underestimating it by a quarter.\n\n## What none of them can tell you\n\n![Banner of an empty scorecard: no vendor publishes a first-attempt merge rate](https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/54b81b237393d8e81463c55c/286cac40-04da-40d9-8985-4ba239050caf.png align=\"center\")\n\nNo vendor in this category publishes a first-attempt merge rate. Not Devin, not Factory, not 8090, not FactoryKit. There is no cross-vendor benchmark for ticket-to-merged-PR reliability, which means every claim on this page, including ours, is unmeasured against a shared standard.\n\nSo evaluate on evidence per run, not on claims. Three questions do most of the work:\n\n1.  **What arrives attached to the pull request?** Check results, a browser recording, a diff review, or just an assertion that it worked.\n    \n2.  **Where do credentials live during a run?** If the answer is inside the sandbox with the agent, keep asking.\n    \n3.  **What does a failed run cost?** Retries bill at full token price, so cost per finished task is the number to track, not cost per run.\n    \n\n## FAQ\n\n![Banner with a question mark keycap introducing frequently asked questions about AI software factories](https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/54b81b237393d8e81463c55c/272bd556-44e4-44f4-8128-6895692ae364.png align=\"center\")\n\n### What is the difference between an AI software factory and a coding agent?\n\nWhere the human stands. A coding agent needs you in the session, steering, which is the whole experience of running Claude Code or Codex in your terminal. A factory wants you at exactly one point: reviewing the pull request. The agent is a component of the factory, not a substitute for it, which is why tier 2 above treats it as one layer of five.\n\n### Can I build one from tools I already pay for?\n\nYes, and that is what tier 2 is. If you already have a coding agent subscription, a CI provider, and a ticket tracker, you have three of the five stages. What you are missing is isolation, credential brokering, and the joins between them. Ramp and Uber both built exactly this, so it is a proven path with a known price.\n\n### What does an AI software factory cost to run?\n\nTwo meters. The platform, which depending on the tier is priced per seat, per usage, or as an engagement. And the model tokens underneath, which scale with parallelism and with retries, since a run that fails its checks and fixes itself pays for every attempt. A factory that needs three attempts per ticket costs triple its demo.\n\n### Is a DoD software factory the same thing?\n\nNo. Kessel Run, Platform One, and the other accredited Department of Defense software factories are DevSecOps platforms: golden pipelines, hardened containers, continuous authority to operate. They industrialise delivery and compliance, and humans still write the code. The two meanings share a name and an ancestor, not an architecture.\n\n### What is a forward-deployed engineer?\n\nA forward-deployed engineer (FDE) is an engineer who embeds with a customer to deploy and adapt a product inside the customer's own environment, rather than supporting it from the outside. The model [comes from Palantir](https://factorykit.ai/p/forward-deployed-engineers) and has spread through enterprise AI companies because integration, not software, is where their deployments succeed or fail. In this category, FDE-led means the factory is installed on your infrastructure, run on your real backlog, and handed to your team.\n\n### Do I need a sandbox, or is CI enough?\n\nCI runs your checks against a diff that already exists. A factory needs somewhere for an agent to work before the diff exists: to install dependencies, run the app, break things, and try again. That is a different requirement, and running it on CI infrastructure means giving a non-deterministic process the credentials and network access your CI holds.\n","html":"\u003cp\u003etldr: An AI software factory takes a ticket to a reviewed pull request with no human in the middle. There are four ways to get one: buy a platform, assemble it from parts, self-host the stack, or have one built and operated inside your environment. Ramp and Uber built theirs with platform teams. Here is what each route costs in engineering time.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch2\u003eWhat an AI software factory is made of\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cimg src=\"https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/54b81b237393d8e81463c55c/debc201b-79d0-4fd7-817f-b07564d275a3.png\" alt=\"Banner of the factory line: a ticket feeds sandbox, agent, and QA stations and comes out as a pull request with evidence\" style=\"display:block;margin:0 auto\" /\u003e\n\n\u003cp\u003eEvery product in this category runs the same five-stage loop, so it is the most useful way to organise the tooling.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eIntake.\u003c/strong\u003e Work arrives as a ticket, spec, or logged bug rather than as a prompt typed into an editor.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eIsolation.\u003c/strong\u003e A sandbox spins up, clones the repositories, and is destroyed when the run ends.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eImplementation.\u003c/strong\u003e A coding agent does the work inside that sandbox.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eVerification.\u003c/strong\u003e The run executes the repository's own checks, and for user-facing changes drives a real browser.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eThe pull request.\u003c/strong\u003e One PR per changed repository, with the diff and the evidence attached. A human reviews and merges.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\n\u003cimg src=\"https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/54b81b237393d8e81463c55c/22d42980-de73-4649-9875-8a7fe481ac4d.png\" alt=\"The AI software factory loop: intake from Linear, Jira, or GitHub Issues, an isolated sandbox, a coding agent implementing the change, verification through repo checks and recorded browser QA with a retry loop on failure, and one evidence-backed pull request per changed repo for human review\" style=\"display:block;margin:0 auto\" /\u003e\n\n\u003cp\u003eWe covered the category argument and who is claiming what in \u003ca href=\"https://hashnode.com/blog/ai-software-factory\"\u003ea separate piece on the AI software factory\u003c/a\u003e. This one is about the parts.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eOne disambiguation before the tools. If you arrived here from a government or defence context, \"software factory\" there still means the 2010s DevSecOps meaning: accredited platforms and teams like Kessel Run and Platform One, with golden pipelines and continuous authority to operate. Humans still write the software in those. Same name, different architecture, and the rest of this article is about the agent-era sense.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch2\u003eThe teams who built their own\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cimg src=\"https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/54b81b237393d8e81463c55c/c3ba3b93-ea9d-47b7-ac87-ae6a48903df0.png\" alt=\"Banner naming the two in-house software factories: Ramp's Inspect and Uber's Minion\" style=\"display:block;margin:0 auto\" /\u003e\n\n\u003cp\u003eTwo things are worth knowing before you evaluate anything, because they establish that this works and what it costs.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eRamp built an internal background coding agent called Inspect. Their engineering post states that \u003ca href=\"https://builders.ramp.com/post/why-we-built-our-background-agent\"\u003e~30% of all pull requests merged to their frontend and backend repos are written by Inspect\u003c/a\u003e. The architecture is worth reading directly: each session runs in a sandboxed VM on Modal \"with everything an engineer would have locally: Vite, Postgres, Temporal, the works,\" from repository images pre-built every 30 minutes, with filesystem snapshots to freeze and restore state.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eUber built Minion, an agent platform wired into their monorepo. Their published figures via The Pragmatic Engineer put \u003ca href=\"https://newsletter.pragmaticengineer.com/p/how-uber-uses-ai-for-development\"\u003e92% of Uber devs using agents monthly and 11% of pull requests opened by agents\u003c/a\u003e. The detailed Minion numbers sit behind that newsletter's paywall, so treat anything more specific you see quoted elsewhere with suspicion.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eNeither company bought this. There was nothing to buy. Both assigned platform teams to build agent infrastructure: sandboxing, credential handling, and review workflow. It worked, which is the useful part. The software factory model is proven. What the two cases also establish is the price of the proof: a platform team.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eKeep that in mind through the next three sections, because the tiers below are mostly a question of who does that work.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch2\u003eTier 1: buy a platform\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cimg src=\"https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/54b81b237393d8e81463c55c/83983791-7dd1-4310-95c0-3c51f7c68d54.png\" alt=\"Banner for tier 1, buying an AI software factory platform off the shelf\" style=\"display:block;margin:0 auto\" /\u003e\n\n\u003cp\u003eThe turnkey option. Every claim in this table is the vendor's own, taken from their site, and none of it is independently measured.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ctable\u003e\n\u003cthead\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\n\u003cth\u003eProduct\u003c/th\u003e\n\u003cth\u003eCompany\u003c/th\u003e\n\u003cth\u003eTheir pitch, their words\u003c/th\u003e\n\u003cth\u003eDeployment\u003c/th\u003e\n\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003c/thead\u003e\n\u003ctbody\u003e\u003ctr\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://cognition.com\"\u003eDevin\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003eCognition\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003e\"The first autonomous software engineer\"\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003eEnterprise; named customers include Goldman Sachs and Mercedes-Benz\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://factory.ai\"\u003eFactory\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003eFactory\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003e\"A self-improving system for your SDLC\"\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003eSaaS, hybrid, on-prem, air-gapped\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://8090.ai\"\u003e8090\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003e8090\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003e\"The AI-native software factory for regulated enterprises\"\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003eSelf-serve platform plus custom enterprise builds\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003c/tbody\u003e\u003c/table\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThere is also a lighter version of this tier hiding inside subscriptions you may already pay for. \u003ca href=\"https://github.blog/changelog/2025-09-25-copilot-coding-agent-is-now-generally-available/\"\u003eGitHub Copilot's coding agent\u003c/a\u003e has been generally available since September 2025: assign an issue to Copilot and it works in a cloud environment and returns a draft pull request, with a Linear integration added since. \u003ca href=\"https://jules.google/\"\u003eJules\u003c/a\u003e, Google's asynchronous coding agent, reached general availability at I/O 2026 and runs the same shape, task in, cloud VM, plan, PR out. Cursor runs background agents in its cloud as well. None of these carries the verification or credential plumbing of the dedicated platforms, but if the question is whether the ticket-to-PR loop fits your team at all, the cheapest experiment is one you already own.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eWhat you are buying from the dedicated platforms is the plumbing between the five stages. What you are not buying is the integration into your stack: your repositories, your CI, your ticketing conventions, your compliance posture. That work stays with you, and on a large codebase it is not small.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch2\u003eTier 2: assemble it from parts\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cimg src=\"https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/54b81b237393d8e81463c55c/5da1e1b4-bb5d-494c-8e45-8590416c3e42.png\" alt=\"Banner for tier 2, assembling a software factory from sandbox, agent, and QA parts\" style=\"display:block;margin:0 auto\" /\u003e\n\n\u003cp\u003eThis is what Ramp and Uber did, and every layer of it is now purchasable separately. If you already pay for a coding agent and a CI provider, you are further along than you think.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cimg src=\"https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/54b81b237393d8e81463c55c/16527615-c8b7-420a-98b9-85d8749f66ca.png\" alt=\"The assemble-it-yourself software factory stack by layer: intake tools, agent sandboxes including E2B, Modal, Daytona, Northflank, and Vercel Sandbox, coding agents, verification with repo checks, Playwright, and Passmark, with credentials and orchestration brokered in from outside the flow\" style=\"display:block;margin:0 auto\" /\u003e\n\n\u003ch3\u003eIntake\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eLinear, Jira, GitHub Issues, or a Slack channel. There is no specialist tool here, and that is the point: the queue you already run is the queue the factory reads. The engineering work is in the trigger, deciding which labels or states hand a ticket to an agent.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch3\u003eIsolation\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe agent sandbox is the layer teams underestimate, and the one Ramp singles out in their own writeup.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ctable\u003e\n\u003cthead\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\n\u003cth\u003eSandbox\u003c/th\u003e\n\u003cth\u003eWhat it is built for\u003c/th\u003e\n\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003c/thead\u003e\n\u003ctbody\u003e\u003ctr\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://e2b.dev\"\u003eE2B\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003eIsolated sandboxes for agents to execute code, each a Linux VM created on demand\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://modal.com\"\u003eModal\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003eSecure containers for running untrusted user or agent code, defined at runtime instead of pre-deployed. This is what Ramp runs Inspect on\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://daytona.io\"\u003eDaytona\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003eDevelopment environments that persist across sessions instead of being torn down each run\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://northflank.com\"\u003eNorthflank\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003eSandboxes for untrusted code with managed cloud or your own VPC\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://vercel.com/docs/vercel-sandbox\"\u003eVercel Sandbox\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003eEphemeral sandboxes for running untrusted, agent-generated code on Vercel's infrastructure\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003c/tbody\u003e\u003c/table\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eA note on sourcing. Most of the head-to-head comparisons of these providers that rank on search are published by Northflank, which is one of the providers in the table. Their posts are useful and also not neutral. The specific isolation technology each uses (microVMs, gVisor, containers) is claimed more precisely in those comparisons than in the providers' own documentation, so verify against primary docs before you make a security decision on it.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch3\u003eImplementation\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe agent that writes the code. Claude Code, Codex, and Grok cover the commercial end, and if you want to see how the first two differ in practice, FactoryKit's learn library \u003ca href=\"https://factorykit.ai/p/claude-code-vs-codex\"\u003ecompares Claude Code and Codex\u003c/a\u003e from the vantage point of running both in production. On the open-source end sit Aider, Cline, OpenCode, \u003ca href=\"https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands\"\u003eOpenHands\u003c/a\u003e, and \u003ca href=\"https://github.com/block/goose\"\u003eGoose\u003c/a\u003e, the Apache 2.0 agent Block built and has since moved to the Linux Foundation.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe useful design decision here is not which agent to pick but whether to pick one at all. Models leapfrog each other on a timescale of weeks, and a factory that hard-codes one agent inherits that model's bad quarter.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch3\u003eVerification\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe stage that separates a factory from an agent left running overnight, and the one most assembled stacks skip.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eRunning the repository's existing checks is the floor: lint, types, unit tests, whatever CI already does. The gap is everything a reviewer actually worries about, which is whether a user-facing change still works. \u003ca href=\"https://playwright.dev\"\u003ePlaywright\u003c/a\u003e is the standard browser automation layer. \u003ca href=\"https://github.com/bug0inc/passmark\"\u003ePassmark\u003c/a\u003e is an open-source Playwright library for AI browser regression testing, with caching, auto-healing, and multi-model verification of assertions, which is the piece that makes browser QA survive a codebase that changes daily.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eGreen unit tests do not tell a reviewer whether the page a user sees still renders. Browser evidence does, and it is the part an assembled stack has to add deliberately.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch3\u003eCredentials\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eInfisical, Doppler, or HashiCorp Vault will hold secrets. The architectural question matters more than the tool: does the agent ever hold a credential at all, or does something outside the sandbox attach them to outbound requests?\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eAn agent with repository write access and a model key is a service with unusual reach and unpredictable behaviour. The \u003ca href=\"https://factorykit.ai/p/coding-agent-security\"\u003ecoding agent security\u003c/a\u003e primer in FactoryKit's learn library covers the threat model, and the short version is that scoping matters more than sandboxing.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch3\u003eOrchestration\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eRetries, long-running runs, and state that survives a process restart. Temporal is the common answer, and notably it appears inside Ramp's sandbox image as well.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch3\u003eWhat assembling actually costs\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eEvery component above is available and most are good. The work is not in choosing them, it is in the joins: trigger logic, credential brokering, snapshot management, retry policy, and the review surface. That is a platform engineering project, it does not finish when the first run succeeds, and Ramp and Uber are the evidence for its scale rather than an argument against doing it.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch2\u003eTier 3: self-host the whole stack\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cimg src=\"https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/54b81b237393d8e81463c55c/7005a971-6c79-4e4e-ae59-4930a12966b4.png\" alt=\"Banner for tier 3, a self-hosted software factory running inside your own network perimeter\" style=\"display:block;margin:0 auto\" /\u003e\n\n\u003cp\u003eFor teams whose code cannot go to a third party at all, whether for regulatory reasons or contractual ones.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eFor a self-hosted coding agent there are real open-source options: Aider, Cline, and OpenCode run against your own model keys, Goose runs entirely on your machine, and OpenHands ships an enterprise Kubernetes deployment. The isolation layer means running Firecracker, gVisor, or Kata Containers yourself rather than buying a sandbox service. Verification and orchestration are unchanged, since Playwright, Passmark, and Temporal are self-hostable already.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eWhat you gain is that nothing leaves your network. What you pay is that you now operate a microVM fleet in addition to everything in tier 2. This is the most expensive route in engineering time and the only viable one for some buyers.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch2\u003eTier 4: have one built by forward-deployed engineers\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cimg src=\"https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/54b81b237393d8e81463c55c/4002052f-32ee-4b2f-abb2-1033c55c82ba.png\" alt=\"Banner for tier 4, a forward-deployed engineering team installing a factory inside your infrastructure\" style=\"display:block;margin:0 auto\" /\u003e\n\n\u003cp\u003eThe fourth route is the one the category rarely names, and it is a different axis from the first three rather than a fourth product.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eA forward-deployed engineer is an engineer who embeds with a customer to deploy and adapt a product inside the customer's own environment, rather than supporting it from the outside. Applied to this category, it means the vendor's engineers install the factory on your infrastructure, run it against your backlog, and hand it over.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eIn tiers 1, 2, and 3, the integration work belongs to the customer. A turnkey platform still has to be wired into your repositories and conventions. Assembling means building those joins. Self-hosting means building them and running the infrastructure underneath. At enterprise scale that integration is not the last mile, it is most of the project: which repos, which CI, which ticketing conventions, which compliance regime, where credentials are allowed to live. A platform ships the generic majority of a factory. The part that decides whether it gets used is specific to the buyer, and that is the part an embedded engineer builds.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe forward-deployed model moves both the integration and the operating burden to the vendor, inside the customer's environment, with custom builds part of the engagement rather than a roadmap item. This is what a software factory as a service properly means, and it is the difference between buying a factory and having one installed.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThree properties make the model work for enterprises in a way the other tiers cannot. The factory runs in your cloud or fully on premises, so the data objection that disqualifies tier 1 for regulated buyers does not arise. The backlog is being cleared while the factory is being built, which no tier 2 project can offer, since those spend their first quarter shipping nothing but infrastructure. And the engagement is designed to end: the vendor's engineers hand the controls to your team and stay on maintenance, so what you own at the end is a factory, not a dependency on the people who built it.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cimg src=\"https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/54b81b237393d8e81463c55c/c9ab6c59-ac0f-4f36-97f1-8989628ceeaf.png\" alt=\"The FactoryKit homepage: Ramp and Uber built their own coding-agent factories, you can just plug one in. The subhead describes plain-language tasks becoming evidence-backed pull requests, implemented by an isolated AI coding agent and QA'd in a recorded real browser\" style=\"display:block;margin:0 auto\" /\u003e\n\n\u003cp\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://factorykit.ai\"\u003eFactoryKit\u003c/a\u003e, which is built by the team behind this publication, runs exactly this model: its forward-deployed engineers drive the factory on the customer's backlog for the first one to three months while it is built on their infrastructure, then hand it over and stay on maintenance under subscription. The architecture underneath:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cp\u003eEach task runs in an isolated cloud sandbox. No local development environment is involved.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe coding agent is chosen per task: Claude Code, Codex, or Grok.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe agent never holds a real credential. Credentials are brokered into outbound traffic in transit, scoped per repository.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe agent never touches git. The platform commits, pushes, and opens one pull request per changed repository, so a multi-repo task returns coordinated PRs instead of one tangled diff.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cp\u003eEvery user-facing change is regression tested in a real browser with Passmark, and the session recording is attached to the pull request.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cp\u003eLinear is connected today: label an issue, and the factory picks it up and answers on the ticket with a PR.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\n\u003cimg src=\"https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/54b81b237393d8e81463c55c/9f22522f-2607-4b68-887b-388750de423a.png\" alt=\"A FactoryKit task that touched several repositories, showing one pull request opened in each changed repository rather than a single combined diff\" style=\"display:block;margin:0 auto\" /\u003e\n\n\u003cp\u003eThe recording is the part that is hard to picture from a bullet, so here is what actually lands on the pull request: the browser QA session for the change, attached to the PR a reviewer opens.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cimg src=\"https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/54b81b237393d8e81463c55c/9b0b179f-2b23-44d1-a698-2cf8cb9ef9b6.png\" alt=\"A FactoryKit pull request with the browser QA session recording attached, showing the regression test of the change as evidence for the reviewer\" style=\"display:block;margin:0 auto\" /\u003e\n\n\u003cp\u003eThe limits. Standard web applications are the sweet spot and mobile is not supported. It is GitHub only, so GitLab teams are out for now. FactoryKit's own numbers put simple tasks at about five minutes, moderate ones at ten to fifteen, and complex ones at twenty to thirty. And a vague task produces a vague PR, which is the constraint every product in this category shares and few will print.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch2\u003eWhich route are you actually factory: buy, assemble, self-host, or forward-deployed\" style=\"display:block;margin:0 auto\" Three questions do most of the work:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhat arrives attached to the pull request?\u003c/strong\u003e Check results, a browser recording, a diff review, or just an assertion that it worked.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhere do credentials live during a run?\u003c/strong\u003e If the answer is inside the sandbox with the agent, keep asking.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhat does a failed run cost?\u003c/strong\u003e Retries bill at full token price, so cost per finished task is the number to track, not cost per run.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\n\u003ch2\u003eFAQ\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cimg src=\"https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/54b81b237393d8e81463c55c/272bd556-44e4-44f4-8128-6895692ae364.png\" alt=\"Banner with a question mark keycap introducing frequently asked questions about AI software factories\" style=\"display:block;margin:0 auto\" /\u003e\n\n\u003ch3\u003eWhat is the difference between an AI software factory and a coding agent?\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eWhere the human stands. A coding agent needs you in the session, steering, which is the whole experience of running Claude Code or Codex in your terminal. A factory wants you at exactly one point: reviewing the pull request. The agent is a component of the factory, not a substitute for it, which is why tier 2 above treats it as one layer of five.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch3\u003eCan I build one from tools I already pay for?\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eYes, and that is what tier 2 is. If you already have a coding agent subscription, a CI provider, and a ticket tracker, you have three of the five stages. What you are missing is isolation, credential brokering, and the joins between them. Ramp and Uber both built exactly this, so it is a proven path with a known price.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch3\u003eWhat does an AI software factory cost to run?\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eTwo meters. The platform, which depending on the tier is priced per seat, per usage, or as an engagement. And the model tokens underneath, which scale with parallelism and with retries, since a run that fails its checks and fixes itself pays for every attempt. A factory that needs three attempts per ticket costs triple its demo.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch3\u003eIs a DoD software factory the same thing?\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eNo. Kessel Run, Platform One, and the other accredited Department of Defense software factories are DevSecOps platforms: golden pipelines, hardened containers, continuous authority to operate. They industrialise delivery and compliance, and humans still write the code. The two meanings share a name and an ancestor, not an architecture.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch3\u003eWhat is a forward-deployed engineer?\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eA forward-deployed engineer (FDE) is an engineer who embeds with a customer to deploy and adapt a product inside the customer's own environment, rather than supporting it from the outside. The model \u003ca href=\"https://factorykit.ai/p/forward-deployed-engineers\"\u003ecomes from Palantir\u003c/a\u003e and has spread through enterprise AI companies because integration, not software, is where their deployments succeed or fail. In this category, FDE-led means the factory is installed on your infrastructure, run on your real backlog, and handed to your team.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch3\u003eDo I need a sandbox, or is CI enough?\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eCI runs your checks against a diff that already exists. A factory needs somewhere for an agent to work before the diff exists: to install dependencies, run the app, break things, and try again. That is a different requirement, and running it on CI infrastructure means giving a non-deterministic process the credentials and network access your CI holds.\u003c/p\u003e\n"},"ogMetaData":{"image":"https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/54b81b237393d8e81463c55c/2a673ac8-d4ea-4d22-b527-1bba0ed7c93f.png"},"tags":[{"id":"660a2928a10ebc3d3a8ffa6c","name":"AI coding","slug":"ai-coding"},{"id":"6a463a8846ccf1cb41b7177d","name":"software-factory","slug":"software-factory"},{"id":"68f0c115c58a29b9d5df3a5d","name":"coding agents","slug":"coding-agents"},{"id":"57ebac0bd9b08ec06a77be05","name":"Developer Tools","slug":"developer-tools"},{"id":"63ec0c658dd6c5e9122eadc4","name":"ai agents","slug":"ai-agents"}],"features":{"tableOfContents":{"isEnabled":false,"items":[]}},"preferences":{"disableComments":false},"comments":{"edges":[{"node":{"id":"6a71ddbb84d3183f629bae4c","dateAdded":"2026-08-04T12:40:27.069Z","totalReactions":0,"content":{"markdown":"I think the assembly route will be where a lot of startups start.\nThe pieces exist already, the hard part is connecting them into a reliable workflow."},"author":{"name":"Julian Neagu","username":"julianneagulab","profilePicture":"https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/avatars/6a249f3d85227ad88016110a/20ab2d8a-8738-42c0-83fa-4d76b93e3562.jpg","tagline":"500+ AI tools shipped solo. https://hashnode.com/blog/ai-software-fa.visible_text: AI software factory tools in 2026: platforms, parts, and self-hosted options AI Coding Infrastructure Quality Startups About AI software factory tools in 2026: buy one, assemble one, or have one built Ramp and Uber built theirs with platform teams. There are now four ways to get a factory that turns tickets into reviewed pull requests, and they differ mostly in who does the integration work. Syed Fazle Rahman · Jul 31, 2026 · 17 min read tldr: An AI software factory takes a ticket to a reviewed pull request with no human in the middle. There are four ways to get one: buy a platform, assemble it from parts, self-host the stack, or have one built and operated inside your environment. Ramp and Uber built theirs with platform teams. Here is what each route costs in engineering time. What an AI software factory is made of Every product in this category runs the same five-stage loop, so it is the most useful way to organise the tooling. Intake. Work arrives as a ticket, spec, or logged bug rather than as a prompt typed into an editor. Isolation. A sandbox spins up, clones the repositories, and is destroyed when the run ends. Implementation. A coding agent does the work inside that sandbox. Verification. The run executes the repository's own checks, and for user-facing changes drives a real browser. The pull request. One PR per changed repository, with the diff and the evidence attached. A human reviews and merges. We covered the category argument and who is claiming what in a separate piece on the AI software factory . This one is about the parts. One disambiguation before the tools. If you arrived here from a government or defence context, "software factory" there still means the 2010s DevSecOps meaning: accredited platforms and teams like Kessel Run and Platform One, with golden pipelines and continuous authority to operate. Humans still write the software in those. Same name, different architecture, and the rest of this article is about the agent-era sense. The teams who built their own Two things are worth knowing before you evaluate anything, because they establish that this works and what it costs. Ramp built an internal background coding agent called Inspect. Their engineering post states that ~30% of all pull requests merged to their frontend and backend repos are written by Inspect . The architecture is worth reading directly: each session runs in a sandboxed VM on Modal "with everything an engineer would have locally: Vite, Postgres, Temporal, the works," from repository images pre-built every 30 minutes, with filesystem snapshots to freeze and restore state. Uber built Minion, an agent platform wired into their monorepo. Their published figures via The Pragmatic Engineer put 92% of Uber devs using agents monthly and 11% of pull requests opened by agents . The detailed Minion numbers sit behind that newsletter's paywall, so treat anything more specific you see quoted elsewhere with suspicion. Neither company bought this. There was nothing to buy. Both assigned platform teams to build agent infrastructure: sandboxing, credential handling, and review workflow. It worked, which is the useful part. The software factory model is proven. What the two cases also establish is the price of the proof: a platform team. Keep that in mind through the next three sections, because the tiers below are mostly a question of who does that work. Tier 1: buy a platform The turnkey option. Every claim in this table is the vendor's own, taken from their site, and none of it is independently measured. Product Company Their pitch, their words Deployment Devin Cognition "The first autonomous software engineer" Enterprise; named customers include Goldman Sachs and Mercedes-Benz Factory Factory "A self-improving system for your SDLC" SaaS, hybrid, on-prem, air-gapped 8090 8090 "The AI-native software factory for regulated enterprises" Self-serve platform plus custom enterprise builds There is also a lighter version of this tier hiding inside subscriptions you may already pay for. GitHub Copilot's coding agent has been generally available since September 2025: assign an issue to Copilot and it works in a cloud environment and returns a draft pull request, with a Linear integration added since. Jules , Google's asynchronous coding agent, reached general availability at I/O 2026 and runs the same shape, task in, cloud VM, plan, PR out. Cursor runs background agents in its cloud as well. None of these carries the verification or credential plumbing of the dedicated platforms, but if the question is whether the ticket-to-PR loop fits your team at all, the cheapest experiment is one you already own. What you are buying from the dedicated platforms is the plumbing between the five stages. What you are not buying is the integration into your stack: your repositories, your CI, your ticketing conventions, your compliance posture. That work stays with you, and on a large codebase it is not small. Tier 2: assemble it from parts This is what Ramp and Uber did, and every layer of it is now purchasable separately. If you already pay for a coding agent and a CI provider, you are further along than you think. Intake Linear, Jira, GitHub Issues, or a Slack channel. There is no specialist tool here, and that is the point: the queue you already run is the queue the factory reads. The engineering work is in the trigger, deciding which labels or states hand a ticket to an agent. Isolation The agent sandbox is the layer teams underestimate, and the one Ramp singles out in their own writeup. Sandbox What it is built for E2B Isolated sandboxes for agents to execute code, each a Linux VM created on demand Modal Secure containers for running untrusted user or agent code, defined at runtime instead of pre-deployed. This is what Ramp runs Inspect on Daytona Development environments that persist across sessions instead of being torn down each run Northflank Sandboxes for untrusted code with managed cloud or your own VPC Vercel Sandbox Ephemeral sandboxes for running untrusted, agent-generated code on Vercel's infrastructure A note on sourcing. Most of the head-to-head comparisons of these providers that rank on search are published by Northflank, which is one of the providers in the table. Their posts are useful and also not neutral. The specific isolation technology each uses (microVMs, gVisor, containers) is claimed more precisely in those comparisons than in the providers' own documentation, so verify against primary docs before you make a security decision on it. Implementation The agent that writes the code. Claude Code, Codex, and Grok cover the commercial end, and if you want to see how the first two differ in practice, FactoryKit's learn library compares Claude Code and Codex from the vantage point of running both in production. On the open-source end sit Aider, Cline, OpenCode, OpenHands , and Goose , the Apache 2.0 agent Block built and has since moved to the Linux Foundation. The useful design decision here is not which agent to pick but whether to pick one at all. Models leapfrog each other on a timescale of weeks, and a factory that hard-codes one agent inherits that model's bad quarter. Verification The stage that separates a factory from an agent left running overnight, and the one most assembled stacks skip. Running the repository's existing checks is the floor: lint, types, unit tests, whatever CI already does. The gap is everything a reviewer actually worries about, which is whether a user-facing change still works. Playwright is the standard browser automation layer. Passmark is an open-source Playwright library for AI browser regression testing, with caching, auto-healing, and multi-model verification of assertions, which is the piece that makes browser QA survive a codebase that changes daily. Green unit tests do not tell a reviewer whether the page a user sees still renders. Browser evidence does, and it is the part an assembled stack has to add deliberately. Credentials Infisical, Doppler, or HashiCorp Vault will hold secrets. The architectural question matters more than the tool: does the agent ever hold a credential at all, or does something outside the sandbox attach them to outbound requests? An agent with repository write access and a model key is a service with unusual reach and unpredictable behaviour. The coding agent security primer in FactoryKit's learn library covers the threat model, and the short version is that scoping matters more than sandboxing. Orchestration Retries, long-running runs, and state that survives a process restart. Temporal is the common answer, and notably it appears inside Ramp's sandbox image as well. What assembling actually costs Every component above is available and most are good. The work is not in choosing them, it is in the joins: trigger logic, credential brokering, snapshot management, retry policy, and the review surface. That is a platform engineering project, it does not finish when the first run succeeds, and Ramp and Uber are the evidence for its scale rather than an argument against doing it. Tier 3: self-host the whole stack For teams whose code cannot go to a third party at all, whether for regulatory reasons or contractual ones. For a self-hosted coding agent there are real open-source options: Aider, Cline, and OpenCode run against your own model keys, Goose runs entirely on your machine, and OpenHands ships an enterprise Kubernetes deployment. The isolation layer means running Firecracker, gVisor, or Kata Containers yourself rather than buying a sandbox service. Verification and orchestration are unchanged, since Playwright, Passmark, and Temporal are self-hostable already. What you gain is that nothing leaves your network. What you pay is that you now operate a microVM fleet in addition to everything in tier 2. This is the most expensive route in engineering time and the only viable one for some buyers. Tier 4: have one built by forward-deployed engineers The fourth route is the one the category rarely names, and it is a different axis from the first three rather than a fourth product. A forward-deployed engineer is an engineer who embeds with a customer to deploy and adapt a product inside the customer's own environment, rather than supporting it from the outside. Applied to this category, it means the vendor's engineers install the factory on your infrastructure, run it against your backlog, and hand it over. In tiers 1, 2, and 3, the integration work belongs to the customer. A turnkey platform still has to be wired into your repositories and conventions. Assembling means building those joins. Self-hosting means building them and running the infrastructure underneath. At enterprise scale that integration is not the last mile, it is most of the project: which repos, which CI, which ticketing conventions, which compliance regime, where credentials are allowed to live. A platform ships the generic majority of a factory. The part that decides whether it gets used is specific to the buyer, and that is the part an embedded engineer builds. The forward-deployed model moves both the integration and the operating burden to the vendor, inside the customer's environment, with custom builds part of the engagement rather than a roadmap item. This is what a software factory as a service properly means, and it is the difference between buying a factory and having one installed. Three properties make the model work for enterprises in a way the other tiers cannot. The factory runs in your cloud or fully on premises, so the data objection that disqualifies tier 1 for regulated buyers does not arise. The backlog is being cleared while the factory is being built, which no tier 2 project can offer, since those spend their first quarter shipping nothing but infrastructure. And the engagement is designed to end: the vendor's engineers hand the controls to your team and stay on maintenance, so what you own at the end is a factory, not a dependency on the people who built it. FactoryKit , which is built by the team behind this publication, runs exactly this model: its forward-deployed engineers drive the factory on the customer's backlog for the first one to three months while it is built on their infrastructure, then hand it over and stay on maintenance under subscription. The architecture underneath: Each task runs in an isolated cloud sandbox. No local development environment is involved. The coding agent is chosen per task: Claude Code, Codex, or Grok. The agent never holds a real credential. Credentials are brokered into outbound traffic in transit, scoped per repository. The agent never touches git. The platform commits, pushes, and opens one pull request per changed repository, so a multi-repo task returns coordinated PRs instead of one tangled diff. Every user-facing change is regression tested in a real browser with Passmark, and the session recording is attached to the pull request. Linear is connected today: label an issue, and the factory picks it up and answers on the ticket with a PR. The recording is the part that is hard to picture from a bullet, so here is what actually lands on the pull request: the browser QA session for the change, attached to the PR a reviewer opens. The limits. Standard web applications are the sweet spot and mobile is not supported. It is GitHub only, so GitLab teams are out for now. FactoryKit's own numbers put simple tasks at about five minutes, moderate ones at ten to fifteen, and complex ones at twenty to thirty. And a vague task produces a vague PR, which is the constraint every product in this category shares and few will print. Which route are you actually on Buy a platform Assemble Self-host Forward-deployed Time to first PR Days A quarter Longer Weeks Who integrates it You You You The vendor Who operates it Vendor You You Vendor, in your environment Code leaves your network Yes Depends No No Best fit Speed matters most You have platform engineers Compliance forbids the rest You want tier 2 without building it Most teams evaluating tier 1 are actually choosing between tiers 1 and 4, and most teams evaluating tier 2 are underestimating it by a quarter. What none of them can tell you No vendor in this category publishes a first-attempt merge rate. Not Devin, not Factory, not 8090, not FactoryKit. There is no cross-vendor benchmark for ticket-to-merged-PR reliability, which means every claim on this page, including ours, is unmeasured against a shared standard. So evaluate on evidence per run, not on claims. Three questions do most of the work: What arrives attached to the pull request? Check results, a browser recording, a diff review, or just an assertion that it worked. Where do credentials live during a run? If the answer is inside the sandbox with the agent, keep asking. What does a failed run cost? Retries bill at full token price, so cost per finished task is the number to track, not cost per run. FAQ What is the difference between an AI software factory and a coding agent? Where the human stands. A coding agent needs you in the session, steering, which is the whole experience of running Claude Code or Codex in your terminal. A factory wants you at exactly one point: reviewing the pull request. The agent is a component of the factory, not a substitute for it, which is why tier 2 above treats it as one layer of five. Can I build one from tools I already pay for? Yes, and that is what tier 2 is. If you already have a coding agent subscription, a CI provider, and a ticket tracker, you have three of the five stages. What you are missing is isolation, credential brokering, and the joins between them. Ramp and Uber both built exactly this, so it is a proven path with a known price. What does an AI software factory cost to run? Two meters. The platform, which depending on the tier is priced per seat, per usage, or as an engagement. And the model tokens underneath, which scale with parallelism and with retries, since a run that fails its checks and fixes itself pays for every attempt. A factory that needs three attempts per ticket costs triple its demo. Is a DoD software factory the same thing? No. Kessel Run, Platform One, and the other accredited Department of Defense software factories are DevSecOps platforms: golden pipelines, hardened containers, continuous authority to operate. They industrialise delivery and compliance, and humans still write the code. The two meanings share a name and an ancestor, not an architecture. What is a forward-deployed engineer? A forward-deployed engineer (FDE) is an engineer who embeds with a customer to deploy and adapt a product inside the customer's own environment, rather than supporting it from the outside. The model comes from Palantir and has spread through enterprise AI companies because integration, not software, is where their deployments succeed or fail. In this category, FDE-led means the factory is installed on your infrastructure, run on your real backlog, and handed to your team. Do I need a sandbox, or is CI enough? CI runs your checks against a diff that already exists. A factory needs somewhere for an agent to work before the diff exists: to install dependencies, run the app, break things, and try again. That is a different requirement, and running it on CI infrastructure means giving a non-deterministic process the credentials and network access your CI holds. Aug 2, 2026 The four-tier framing is useful mainly because it makes explicit what most vendor pitches leave implicit: the "buy vs build" question isn't really about capability, it's about who absorbs the integration cost. Tier 1 vendors selling "plug and play" are quietly assuming your repos, CI, and ticketing conventions are generic enough to slot into their plumbing, which is exactly the assumption that breaks on any codebase old enough to have real conventions. The Ramp/Uber framing as "proof the model works, not proof it's cheap" is the right read. Citing both as validation while immediately naming the platform-team cost is more honest than most categoy pieces, which tend to cite the same two companies as evidence you should build in-house without mentioning what building it actually took. The verification section is the one I'd push on hardest in practice, though "green unit tests don't tell a reviewer whether the page still renders" is true, but browser QA with auto-healing assertions has its own failure mode: an auto-healing check that silently adapts to a broken UI state is arguably worse than a hard-failing one, since it launders a regression into "verified" evidence attached to the PR.
